# Generalized Linear Models {#sec-glm} ::: {#cell-setup-08 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using TidierData using DataFrames, CSV using GLM, StatsModels, StatsBase, Statistics, Distributions using MixedModels using CairoMakie CairoMakie.activate!(type = "png") ponds = @chain CSV.read(joinpath("..", "data", "ponds.csv"), DataFrame) begin @drop_missing(canopy) @mutate(log_area = log(area_m2)) end nrow(ponds) ``` ::: {#setup-08 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 173 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note .exercise} ## Exercises in this chapter As in @sec-linear-models, you fit a model in each *Your turn* box and pass a number extracted from it to `check`. Start each session with: ```julia include("exercises/check.jl") using TidierData, DataFrames, CSV, GLM, StatsModels, Statistics, MixedModels ponds = @chain CSV.read(joinpath("data", "ponds.csv"), DataFrame) begin @drop_missing(canopy) @mutate(log_area = log(area_m2)) end ``` ::: ## Why GLMs in ecology {#sec-why-glm} Counts are not normal, proportions live in $[0,1]$, presences are binary. The Gaussian linear model treats all of them as if they were continuous and unbounded, and fails in predictable ways: confidence intervals that include negative richness, misspecified variance, fan-shaped residuals. The GLM fixes this with two choices: the **distribution** of the response and the **link function** connecting the mean to the linear predictor. | Response | Distribution | Link | In Julia | |---|---|---|---| | Count | Poisson | log | `Poisson(), LogLink()` | | Overdispersed count | Negative binomial | log | `negbin(...)` | | Presence/absence | Bernoulli/Binomial | logit | `Binomial(), LogitLink()` | | Proportion with denominator | Binomial | logit | `Binomial(), LogitLink()` | | Positive skewed continuous | Gamma | log | `Gamma(), LogLink()` | ## Poisson: species richness {#sec-poisson} ::: {#cell-glm-poisson .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} g1 = glm(@formula(richness ~ log_area + canopy + temp_c), ponds, Poisson(), LogLink()) ``` ::: {#glm-poisson .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` StatsModels.TableRegressionModel{GeneralizedLinearModel{GLM.GlmResp{Vector{Float64}, Poisson{Float64}, LogLink}, GLM.DensePredChol{Float64, LinearAlgebra.CholeskyPivoted{Float64, Matrix{Float64}, Vector{Int64}}}}, Matrix{Float64}} richness ~ 1 + log_area + canopy + temp_c Coefficients: ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Coef. ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note .exercise} ## Your turn 9.1 — Adding hydroperiod Fit a Poisson GLM like `g1`, adding `hydro` at the end of the formula. Pass its coefficients to `check("9.1", ...)`, then compare its AIC with that of `g1`. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint Copy `g1` and add `+ hydro`. `aic(g)` gives the AIC; lower is better. ::: ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#cell-answer-9-1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} g_hydro = glm(@formula(richness ~ log_area + canopy + temp_c + hydro), ponds, Poisson(), LogLink()) coef(g_hydro) ``` ::: {#answer-9-1 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 5-element Vector{Float64}: -0.2955819444424689 0.3308987450570613 -0.011543093000739657 0.04752717672780732 -0.1895805246826413 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-answer-9-1-check .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} check("9.1", coef(g_hydro)) (aic_g1 = aic(g1), aic_hydro = aic(g_hydro)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
✓ Correct!
``` ::: ::: ::: {#answer-9-1-check .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (aic_g1 = 952.9021516391434, aic_hydro = 944.1070557908267) ``` ::: ::: The AIC drops by about 9, so `hydro` earns its place. The simulation added 0.22 to the log mean of permanent ponds; the model estimates −0.19 for temporary ones, the same effect seen from the other side. ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Interpreting coefficients on the log scale A coefficient $\beta$ under a log link means that a one-unit increase in the predictor multiplies the mean by $e^\beta$. For `canopy`: ::: {#cell-interpretation .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} exp(coef(g1)[3]), (exp(coef(g1)[3]) - 1) * 100 ``` ::: {#interpretation .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (0.9885114593513831, -1.148854064861693) ``` ::: ::: That is, each additional percentage point of canopy reduces expected richness by about 1%. ::: ::: {.callout-note .exercise} ## Your turn 9.2 — Temporary ponds, in plain numbers Using the model from 9.1, by what factor does expected richness change in a temporary pond compared with a permanent one, all else equal? Pass that factor to `check("9.2", ...)`. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint The `hydro: temporary` coefficient is the fifth. Under a log link, a coefficient $\beta$ multiplies the mean by $e^\beta$. ::: ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#cell-answer-9-2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} factor_temp = exp(coef(g_hydro)[5]) ``` ::: {#answer-9-2 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 0.8273060956543652 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#answer-9-2-check .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} check("9.2", factor_temp) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
✓ Correct!
``` ::: ::: ::: About 0.83: temporary ponds are expected to hold about 17% fewer species than permanent ones. ::: ::: ## Overdispersion {#sec-overdispersion} The Poisson assumes $\text{Var}(Y) = \text{E}(Y)$. Ecological data rarely cooperate. ::: {#cell-dispersion .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} # Pearson residual: (y - mu) / sqrt(Var(mu)). For the Poisson, Var(mu) = mu. mu = predict(g1) pearson_res = (ponds.richness .- mu) ./ sqrt.(mu) df_res = dof_residual(g1) phi = sum(pearson_res .^ 2) / df_res (dispersion_statistic = phi, verdict = phi > 1.5 ? "overdispersed" : "acceptable") ``` ::: {#dispersion .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (dispersion_statistic = 1.952703419456855, verdict = "overdispersed") ``` ::: ::: If $\hat\phi \gg 1$, the alternatives are the negative binomial or a mixed model with an observation-level random effect. ::: {.callout-important} ## Overdispersion is a symptom, not a diagnosis `ponds.csv` was generated as a *pure* Poisson process — there is no extra-Poisson variance in the data-generating code. Yet $\hat\phi \approx 1.95$. Why? Because the generating model included a region effect that `g1` omits. Unmodelled heterogeneity inflates the dispersion statistic exactly as genuine overdispersion does, and the statistic cannot tell you which one you have. This matters practically: the reflex of reaching for a negative binomial whenever $\hat\phi > 1.5$ can paper over a missing predictor. Check your model structure before you change your distribution. The GLMM in @sec-glmm addresses the actual cause here. ::: ::: {.callout-note .exercise} ## Your turn 9.3 — Testing the warning The box above claims that the overdispersion of `g1` comes from a missing predictor. Test it: fit a Poisson GLM with `log_area`, `canopy`, `temp_c`, `hydro` and `region`, compute its dispersion statistic as in the block above, and pass it to `check("9.3", ...)`. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint Copy the dispersion block, replacing `g1` with your model. `predict(g)` gives the fitted means. ::: ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#cell-answer-9-3 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} g_full = glm(@formula(richness ~ log_area + canopy + temp_c + hydro + region), ponds, Poisson(), LogLink()) mu_full = predict(g_full) phi_full = sum(((ponds.richness .- mu_full) ./ sqrt.(mu_full)) .^ 2) / dof_residual(g_full) ``` ::: {#answer-9-3 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 0.9410041742922786 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#answer-9-3-check .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} check("9.3", phi_full) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
✓ Correct!
``` ::: ::: ::: About 0.94: with the predictors of the generating model in place, the "overdispersion" is gone. Adding `hydro` alone (9.1) barely moved it; `region` was the missing piece. ::: ::: ::: {#cell-negbin .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} g2 = negbin(@formula(richness ~ log_area + canopy + temp_c), ponds, LogLink()) ``` ::: {#negbin .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` StatsModels.TableRegressionModel{GeneralizedLinearModel{GLM.GlmResp{Vector{Float64}, NegativeBinomial{Float64}, LogLink}, GLM.DensePredChol{Float64, LinearAlgebra.CholeskyPivoted{Float64, Matrix{Float64}, Vector{Int64}}}}, Matrix{Float64}} richness ~ 1 + log_area + canopy + temp_c Coefficients: ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Coef. Compute the odds ratio for an increase of **10** percentage points, from `g4`, and pass it to `check("9.4", ...)`. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint Ten points multiply the odds by $e^{10\beta}$, not by $10\,e^{\beta}$. ::: ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#cell-answer-9-4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} or_10 = exp(10 * coef(g4)[2]) ``` ::: {#answer-9-4 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 1.1881878414800107 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#answer-9-4-check .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} check("9.4", or_10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
✓ Correct!
``` ::: ::: ::: About 1.19: each extra 10 points of canopy multiply the odds of finding the focal species by 1.19, an increase of 19%. ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-logistic .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} grid = DataFrame( canopy = repeat(range(0, 100, length = 100), 2), temp_c = fill(mean(ponds.temp_c), 200), hydro = repeat(["permanent", "temporary"], inner = 100), ) grid.p = predict(g4, grid) fig = Figure(size = (700, 430)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Canopy cover (%)", ylabel = "P(occurrence)", title = "Focal species") for (h, col) in zip(["permanent", "temporary"], [:steelblue, :darkorange]) sub = grid[grid.hydro .== h, :] lines!(ax, sub.canopy, sub.p, color = col, linewidth = 2.5, label = h) end scatter!(ax, ponds.canopy, Float64.(ponds.focal), color = (:grey40, 0.25)) axislegend(ax, position = :lt) fig ``` ::: {#fig-logistic .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Predicted probability of focal-species occurrence along the canopy gradient. ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note .exercise} ## Your turn 9.5 — Predicting a new pond A temporary pond has 80% canopy and water at 26 °C. According to `g4`, what is the probability of finding the focal species there? Pass it to `check("9.5", ...)`. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint Build a one-row `DataFrame` with the columns `canopy`, `temp_c` and `hydro`, and pass it to `predict(g4, ...)`, as with `grid` above. ::: ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {#cell-answer-9-5 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} new_pond = DataFrame(canopy = [80.0], temp_c = [26.0], hydro = ["temporary"]) p_new = predict(g4, new_pond) ``` ::: {#answer-9-5 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 1-element Vector{Union{Missing, Float64}}: 0.5246412509540388 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#answer-9-5-check .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} check("9.5", p_new) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Gaps you will hit {#sec-glm-gaps} This is the point where being honest is worth more than being enthusiastic. The table below is an assessment as of **August 2026**, made by checking the public package registries; check before concluding that something does not exist. | You need | In R | In Julia today | |---|---|---| | Zero-inflation, hurdle | `glmmTMB`, `pscl` | no mature equivalent | | Beta regression | `betareg`, `glmmTMB` | no mature equivalent | | Additive models (GAM) | `mgcv` | no mature equivalent | | Simulated quantile residuals | `DHARMa` | none; implementable by hand | | Marginal means, contrasts | `emmeans` | `Effects.jl`, partial coverage | | Ordinal regression | `ordinal`, `MASS::polr` | partial coverage | ### The pragmatic escape hatch: `RCall.jl` {#sec-rcall} There is no shame in calling R from inside Julia when the right package only exists there. The workflow stays reproducible, and data crosses the boundary automatically. ::: {#rcall-example .cell execution_count=0} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using RCall @rput ponds # send the DataFrame to R R""" library(mgcv) m <- gam(richness ~ s(canopy) + s(log_area) + region, family = poisson, data = ponds) summary(m) """ ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## Where this leaves you For the repertoire covered by this chapter — Poisson, negative binomial, binomial, gamma, offsets, GLMMs — Julia covers what you need, and this chapter has demonstrated it with executed code. Outside it, `RCall.jl` is the bridge. Naming the boundary clearly serves the reader better than hiding it. ::: ## Challenges {.unnumbered} 1. Compute the dispersion statistic for `g2`. Did the negative binomial fix the overdispersion? After 9.3, would you still choose it? 2. Build the predicted-probability curve of @fig-logistic for each hydroperiod at three temperatures (22, 24.5 and 27 °C). How much does temperature shift the curve? 3. Implement `DHARMa`-style quantile residuals for `g1`: simulate 250 datasets from the fitted model and, for each pond, compute the proportion of simulated values below the observed one. If the model is right, these proportions are uniform. Are they? Repeat for the model from 9.3.
